claims.text: The initial material is an as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy containing a nano-lamellar mixture of L12 and B2 phases.
Cryo-rolling followed by annealing can produce a heterogeneous hierarchical microstructure in the eutectic high-entropy alloy.
The resulting hierarchical microstructure contains fine lamellar regions, ultrafine recrystallized FCC grains, coarse recrystallized FCC grains, and coarse recovered B2 regions.
At cryogenic rolling temperature, the hardness or flow stress of the B2 phase increases substantially more than that of the L12 phase.
The cryogenic increase in the relative hardness difference causes more strain to be partitioned into the L12 phase and less strain to accumulate in the B2 phase than during room-temperature rolling.
Mechanical incompatibility between soft and hard domains produces plastic strain gradients at domain interfaces.
Interface strain gradients generate geometrically necessary dislocations and back-stress strengthening of the soft phase.
Back-stress strengthening delays necking during tensile loading.
Cryo-rolling and annealing can provide a simultaneous strength-and-ductility enhancement.
The treated alloy should have a yield strength of approximately 1437 MPa.
The treated alloy should have an elongation to failure of approximately 14%.
The as-cast baseline has a yield strength of approximately 615 MPa.
The as-cast baseline has an elongation to failure of approximately 17%.
Relative to the stated as-cast baseline, the treatment simultaneously increases both strength and ductility.
The intervention is expected to apply to eutectic high-entropy alloys having nano-lamellar L12 and B2 phases.
The intervention may not apply to other types of high-entropy alloys.
The detailed formation mechanism of the hierarchy and its connection to back-stress strengthening are not fully understood.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis asserts a simultaneous increase in strength and ductility relative to the as-cast baseline, but the stated elongation changes from about 17% in the baseline to about 14% after treatment. This is a decrease, not an increase; the evidence describes the elongation as remaining almost unchanged while strength increases.
